title: Designing Reliable Multi‑Agent Apps with Azure Cosmos DB | OD820

segments.text: JUSTINE COCCHI: Hi, I'm Justine Cocchi,
and I'm a Program Manager on the Azure Cosmos DB team.
I'm joined today by Aayush Kataria,
who's a software engineer also working on Cosmos DB.
We're excited to talk to you today
about designing reliable multi-agent apps
with Azure Cosmos DB, and the example
that we'll use today is a travel assistant,
which is a multi-agent AI application
that helps you plan personalized trips.
One of the functionalities
of our application is a chat feature.
When a user wants to plan a trip, they can start a chat
by saying something like "Plan a trip to Paris."
This first gets routed to our orchestrator agent,
who then can pass the message
to various specialist agents, like the hotel agent.
We can look up memories in Azure Cosmos DB with contacts
that we already have stored about this user.
We can embed the initial query with Azure Open AI,
so that we can turn it into vectors that we can then search
against our existing other metadata, like places
and restaurants and hotels in Paris
that may be useful for our user.
Then we're ready to send our message back with the data
that we found and help them plan their trip.
This is just an example of one turn, and if we look
at the user interaction flow, we can see many pieces of data
that are moving through this user journey, from the message
to the various agents we're talking to, when we're ready
to actually create the trip, and lastly,
we need to extract the memories
so that we can remember what's happened next time the user
comes and logs into our website.
There's various things that we want to focus
on in different parts of the user flow
that will really help us keep the best user experience.
In the beginning, the latency
and personalization is the most important.
We want to make sure the agent remembers key things
about our users and that the responses are very fast.
Otherwise, the user may become frustrated and they may go
to one of our competitor travel sites.
Whereas, in the back half, consistency
and reliability become more important.
We don't want to accidentally double-book a trip
or forget something that we already talked about.
So really keeping in mind the user perspective
as we build our application will help us ensure
that our application is reliable.
Now, I want to zoom in on one thing,
which is the number of agents here.
We've talked about an orchestrator
and some specialists.
I want to hand it off to Aayush who's going to talk more
about the multi-agent pattern
and how it can help us in our application.
AAYUSH KATARIA: Thanks, Justine.
Going over the travel scenario that we'll be discussing today.
Hi, I'm Aayush Kataria.
I'm a software engineer at Azure Cosmos DB.
So let's dive into why multi-agent.
So let's start with what goes wrong when you don't.
So on the left, you see the single-agent problem.
When you have one agent trying
to handle every domain all packed
into a single system prompt, the model gets confused.
It doesn't know which capability to invoke or when.
There's no separation of concerns,
so every change risks breaking something else.
You can't scale or improve any area of expertise
without touching everything.
And as conversations grow longer,
you hit context window limits.
The model starts forgetting earlier parts
of the conversation, leading to inconsistent behavior.
So on the right-hand side, we have the multi-agent solution.
Instead of one monolithic agent, you have specialized agents,
each with a focus prompt and a specific set of tools.
So an orchestrator sits on top, routes the user's request
to the right specialist based on the intent,
so this gives us a few big wins.
So first, each agent has a smaller,
more focused context, so it reasons better.
Second, you can develop and update agents independently.
Adding a new specialist doesn't require touching existing ones.
Third, it's composable.
You can plug in new capabilities
without rewriting the whole system.
So now let's look at how agentic memory works better
than retrieval-augmented generation.
So this is where we get into, I think,
which is the most interesting part of the stock.
That is agentic memory.
So most people are familiar with RAG.
That's retrieval-augmented generation.
You have a knowledge base, you embed documents,
and when a user asks a question, you retrieve the relevant chunks
and feed them to the model.
So it works well for what it does
but has fundamental limitations
when you're building agent-based applications.
So let's walk through the comparison.
Traditional RAG is static.
Your knowledge base is fixed until you explicitly update it.
Agentic memory, on the other hand, is dynamic.
It grows automatically with every interaction.
RAG gives the same results to everyone.
It's searching a shared corpus.
Agentic memory is user specific.
It stores individual preferences and history,
so two different users get completely
different experiences.
RAG retrieves by similarity alone.
Whatever is closest in the embedding space comes back.
Agentic memory uses salient scoring, which factors
in importance, confidence, and resiliency.
RAG doesn't learn from interactions.
It's just a pure lookup.
Agentic memory actively learns and adapts.
Every conversation is an opportunity
to extract new knowledge.
And RAG has no concept of time.
Agentic memory supports cross-session persistence
with TTL policies.
Let's now go over the system architecture
for our travel agent application that we are going to demo
at the later end of the session.
So now let's zoom out and look at the full system architecture.
So everything starts when a message lands
in the orchestrator agent.
This is the front door of our application,

After that, there are specialized agents --

In our multi-agent application,

transfer between different agents, and many more.
The point of MCP is decoupling, so we can update or add tools

It stores everything the application needs, sessions,

Places are searched using hybrid search,

to host your memory layer, so for any multi-agent application.
It is a separate background runtime
that hands off the same Cosmos DB account
that I mentioned before.
It owns its own container called "memories"
where the actual turns of the conversation, facts extracted
from those turns, the user summaries, the thread summaries,
everything is stored, and the agent never calls it directly.
And then we have the Azure OpenAI
which is providing the LLM reasoning
and embedding capabilities.
It's a shared utility that feeds both the agent runtime
and the toolkit pipeline.
Now let's go over some concepts about memory and agentic memory.
So before we go deeper into memory,
let's establish a clear vocabulary.
People use the word "memory" loosely, so let's be precise.
So there are three distinct concepts here.
State, which is the snapshot
of your entire application at any given moment.
It contains everything needed to restore the application
to that exact point, what the user said,
what the agent decided, what tools were called.
Then we have short-term memory, which is what happens
within that particular single session.
It's the conversation history,
the messages going back and forth.
This is what lets an agent refer back
to something the user said three messages ago
and give a coherent response.
Then we have the long-term memory.
This is where things actually start to get more powerful.
This persists across sessions.
When a user comes back days or weeks later,
the agent can recall what it learned about them previously,
their preferences, past decisions, feedback,
and this is what enables personalization
and learning over time.
It's the difference between an agent
that starts fresh every conversation and one
that builds a relationship with the user.

I'm wondering, how can we implement these

that with four different types of memories.
So the reason this matters is each type has a different
lifetime, a different way of being created,
and a different way the agent uses it.
So let's walk through them.
As you can see here, we have a few different types of memory
that we are storing in our agent memory toolkit.
First is the facts, so sometimes called "semantic memory."
These are simple, durable statements about the user.
User is vegetarian, travels with a wheelchair, lives in Seattle.
They are objectively true.
They don't change often and they should never expire.
Second is the procedural memory.
This is behavioral patterns, preferences inferred
from how the user actually behaves
over multiple conversations, tends to book boutique hotels
over chains, prefers late dinners.
These are softer than facts, so the user might never say them
out loud, but they emerge from repetition.
They also never expire by default
because behavioral patterns are usually stable.
Third is episodic memory.
These are tied to a specific time and place.
Visited New York City in last spring,
loved seafood on my Barcelona trip.
These are how the system knows to reference a past trip
when planning a new one, and these do expire.
So the default is 90 days.
Episodic memory gets a little noisy too fast,
and a recommendation system doesn't really need
to remember a coffee shop
that you went probably four years ago.
Fourth is the user summary.
This is different from the other three.
It's not extracted from a single message.
It's a rolling synthesis of who this user I,
regenerated automatically every few turns.
It can be something like
"This user is a frequent solo traveler, vegetarian,
prefers cultural over outdoor, mid-range hotels."
So the orchestrator pulls these into its system prompt
at the start of every conversation.
So even on day one of a brand-new session,
the agent already knows the user.

So the real value comes from making memories intelligent.
So the user never has to say, "Remember this."
As the conversation unfolds,
a background pipeline runs every end turn
in the agent memory toolkit and asks the LLM,
"Is there anything new about this user worth remembering?"
If the user is -- if the answer is yes, it pulls out a fact,
classifies it as a fact, procedural or episodic memory,
and writes it back to Cosmos DB.
The agent loop doesn't wait on this.
It happens asynchronously in the background.
The second piece is conflict resolution, which is done
by the reconciled memories method.
So real conversations always would be contradicting.
The user says "I'm vegan" on Monday.
Three weeks later, they mention how much they love a steakhouse
and they have started eating meat.
So now what does the system do?
So on a separate cadence,
the toolkit periodically sweeps the user's facts
and asks the LLM to classify the pairs of related memories
so they can be either duplicates or updates.
When it finds one, it doesn't delete the user.
It marks it superseded by the winner.
That is done so that the audit trail is preserved,
so the user never sees a contradiction
in the recommendations.
But if you're debugging, say, six months later,
you can still see exactly when
and why the system changed its mind.
The third place is rolling summaries.
Conversations can get long.
Token budgets are finite.
The toolkit handles this by generating two kinds
of summaries on a cadence.
So one is threat summary
that captures the current conversation,
the current session, and the thread,
and other is user summary that captures who this user is
across all conversations.
So just for this demo purposes, both user summary
and threat summary are regenerated
after every five turns, so we can actually see that happen
in the demo in a few minutes.
In production, the agent toolkit has like some default set
which are tunable by the customer who's going
to use the agent memory toolkit.
So the orchestrator eventually pulls these summaries
into context at the start of every turn,
so even after a hundred messages,
the agent doesn't lose the actual plot.
The fourth piece is what I think of as the payoff.
That is memory condition search.
So everything that we've talked about so far is plumbing.
This is where the memory shapes what the user actually sees.
So before any specialist agent searches for a hotel
or a restaurant, it recalls memories first
to ask the toolkit, "What do we know
about this user that's relevant to this particular query?"
So the recall comes back with relevant facts and preferences,
and the agent then encodes those
as explicit filters on the search call.
That's how "Show me hotels in Tokyo" becomes
"Show me luxury hotels in Tokyo."
So the personalization isn't bolted on at the end.
It's baked into the query itself.
So the agent memory toolkit runs all these automatically
